sentences.text: The house at Ferrel is still empty.
The roof went properly in 2019 and there is a tarpaulin on it that Mariana's father put up and that has been there for six years.
The gutter is off the back.
There is a fig growing out of the wall by the chimney that was a seedling when she was fourteen and is now taller than she is.
Mariana goes and looks at it about twice a year.
She has a key.

She goes in and stands in the kitchen where her grandmother made her sit down and drink milk and told her, at nine, what the window cost, and then she comes out and locks it and drives back to Caldas.
The room at the back faces the oaks and the window in it does not open any more, because the frame has gone, and that is the only thing in that house that Mariana is glad about.
Nobody has sold it and nobody has fixed it, and the reason is not that they cannot agree.
The reason is that the question does not come up.
Mariana has watched this for eleven years and she can describe the mechanism exactly, because she has tested it.
She has raised it herself, deliberately, at dinner, four times.

It goes like this: she says the house, and her mother says yes, they must sort that out, and her uncle says the same thing on the phone at Christmas, and everybody agrees entirely, with real warmth, that something ought to be done.
And then it goes.
Not refused.
Not deflected.

It simply does not have any weight — the subject comes up and slides off and the conversation is on to something else, and if you ask anybody afterwards what was decided they will tell you, honestly, that it was a good talk and that they will get to it.
She has tried writing it down and putting it in front of them.
She did that at twenty-one: two pages, the state of the roof, three options with numbers, a recommendation.
Her mother read it and said it was very good and that Mariana had always been the sensible one.
Her uncle read it and rang up and was warm about it for twenty minutes.
Nobody disagreed with a single line of it and nothing happened, and when she brought it up again at Christmas her mother could not remember which of the three options she had preferred.
Her mother and her uncle have not had a cross word in eleven years, which in a Portuguese inheritance is close to a miracle, and everybody in both families says so.
Mariana is twenty-three and she has said this out loud to one person, who was kind about it.
The person was a woman she shared a flat with in Coimbra, who listened to all of it and then asked one question, which was whether Mariana had ever told her mother.
She has not.

She has thought about it perhaps four hundred times and she has worked out that there is no version of that conversation that does not end with her mother going and standing in front of the question for a while and then getting on with the dinner.
What she says is that the ants did exactly what they are asked to do and what her grandmother told her they do, and that nobody in Ferrel has ever misdescribed it.
The argument was taken.
It has not come back and it is not coming back.

What nobody had ever said to her — and she does not think anybody was hiding it, she thinks it is simply not the sort of thing that gets said to a child, and she is not sure she would have heard it at twelve — is that an argument is a thing standing on something.
They took the argument.

The house is what the argument was standing on, and the house is still there, with a fig in the wall, and there is nobody left in that family who can hold the question in their hands for long enough to answer it.
